Change in the paid brand's share of the doctor's GLP-1 claims around the first payment, against not-yet-paid doctors. Data: [switching.json](qa/switching.json).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## What we found

- **After a drug maker's first payment, its GLP-1 brand gains a few percentage points of the doctor's GLP-1 prescribing.** Compared with similar doctors not yet paid, the paid brand's share rises by {{< var share_trulicity >}} points for Trulicity, {{< var share_ozempic >}} for Ozempic and {{< var share_mounjaro >}} for Mounjaro, mostly at the expense of direct competitors.
- **Doctors whose practices were already growing are the ones companies reach.** Paid doctors become more likely to prescribe the paid brand regularly ({{< var att_trulicity >}} / {{< var att_victoza >}} / {{< var att_ozempic >}} percentage points for Trulicity, Victoza and Ozempic), but their statin prescribing, which no GLP-1 payment should touch, rises too ({{< var statin_trulicity >}} / {{< var statin_victoza >}} / {{< var statin_ozempic >}}).
- **The money is concentrated.** Since 2013, drug makers have paid ${{< var promo_usd_m >}} million in promotional payments naming a GLP-1 to about {{< var paid_npis_k >}},000 prescribers; the top 1% received {{< var top1_share >}}% of it, {{< var top1_speaker_share >}}% of that as speaker fees.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## What this doesn't mean

- **It does not show that payments caused prescribing.** Companies choose whom to pay, and they call on doctors when a brand gains formulary or guideline position. The share shift is *consistent with* payments influencing brand choice, but not proof.
- **It is not evidence of inappropriate prescribing.** GLP-1s are effective diabetes drugs; prescribing more of them, or of one brand, can be good care.
- **It says nothing about obesity prescribing** (Medicare Part D excludes weight-loss-only use) **or about any individual doctor.** No prescriber is named, mapped or ranked anywhere in this project.
:::

## The question

Between 2013 and 2024, Medicare Part D spending on GLP-1 drugs grew from ${{< var spend_2013 >}} billion to ${{< var spend_2024 >}} billion a year. Over the same years the companies that make them, chiefly Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, paid doctors for meals, talks, consulting and travel, and the federal Open Payments program published every payment.

Two decades of research find that doctors who take industry money prescribe more of the payer's drugs [@dejong2016; @yeh2016; @fleischman2016; @hadland2018; @mitchell2021]. Almost all of that work compares paid and unpaid doctors at one point in time, so it cannot tell influence from targeting: drug representatives visit the doctors who already prescribe, or are about to prescribe, the most. The one GLP-1 study so far is also a cross-sectional snapshot [@khunte2026].

This project asks a narrower, harder question: **when a doctor receives a first promotional payment for a specific GLP-1 brand, does their prescribing of *that brand* change afterwards, compared with similar doctors who have not yet been paid — and does it change in ways that targeting alone would not produce?**

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart3_partd_spending.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart3_partd_spending >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart3_partd_spending_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart3_partd_spending >}}"}
:::

## The data

Everything here comes from public federal data.

- **CMS Open Payments**, the "Sunshine Act" database: {{< var glp1_records_m >}} million general payments that name a GLP-1 brand, 2013–2025. We keep the promotional ones (meals, speaker and consulting fees, travel, education, gifts) and drop royalties, research grants and acquisitions. A payment naming several drugs is split equally between them for dollar totals.
- **Medicare Part D Prescribers by Provider and Drug**, 2013–2024: each prescriber's yearly claims for each drug, linked to Open Payments by National Provider Identifier. The link is near-complete: {{< var link_2013 >}}% of physician payment records in 2013 and at least {{< var link_2015 >}}% from 2015 on.
- **The analysis panel** follows {{< var n_diabetes >}} prescribers who treat diabetes regularly (out of {{< var n_partd_prescribers >}} Part D prescribers), each GLP-1 brand and each year. The main event study uses the {{< var n_physicians >}} physicians among them, because payments to nurse practitioners and physician assistants were not reported before 2021.

Two features of the data shape every result:

1. **Medicare hides small counts.** A prescriber-drug row with fewer than 11 claims in a year is suppressed. A missing row means "0 to 10 claims", not zero. The main outcome is therefore *whether* a doctor wrote at least 11 claims of the brand that year, which is always observed; prescription volumes are estimated separately with bounds for the hidden cells.
2. **Almost every GLP-1 prescriber gets paid eventually.** {{< var fills_paid_2013 >}}% of GLP-1 fills in 2013, and {{< var fills_paid_2024 >}}% in 2024, came from prescribers who received a GLP-1 payment at some point. So the comparison group is mostly doctors **not paid yet**, not doctors never paid.

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart4_payments_by_type.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart4_payments_by_type >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart4_payments_by_type_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart4_payments_by_type >}}"}
:::

## How we measured it, in plain English

**Before looking at any result, we wrote down the analysis and locked it.** The pre-registration ([PREREGISTRATION.md](https://github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1/blob/main/PREREGISTRATION.md)) fixed the outcome, the comparison, the estimator, the tests that could prove the finding wrong, and how each pattern of results would be described. Every later change is logged there as a dated deviation.

**The comparison.** For each brand, doctors enter the study in the year of their first promotional payment for it. Each one is compared with doctors in the same years who had not yet been paid for that brand, and who had a similar diabetes workload, overall Medicare volume, prior GLP-1 prescribing, specialty and region. The estimator, from @callaway2021 with the doubly robust adjustment of @santanna2020, is built for exactly this staggered timing; simpler two-way fixed-effects regressions can give badly wrong answers when timing varies [@goodmanbacon2021; @roth2023].

**The tests that could sink it.** If payments simply mark doctors who were already on the way up, three things should show:

- **a rising trend *before* the first payment** (checked with pre-period estimates and the sensitivity bounds of @rambachan2023);
- **the same "effect" on drugs the payment has nothing to do with**, here statins (a *negative-control outcome*, @lipsitch2010);
- **an effect that disappears when paid doctors are matched to unpaid doctors with the same prior trajectory** [coarsened exact matching, @iacus2012].

**Brand share.** The cleanest test asks how the paid brand's *share* of the doctor's own GLP-1 prescribing changes. A doctor whose practice is simply growing should prescribe more of every brand, so share cancels practice size out, in the spirit of @dejong2016.

**Who this describes.** Nearly all newly paid doctors were first reached through sponsored meals: {{< var share_under_100 >}}% received under $100 in their first payment year. The {{< var glp1_speakers >}} doctors ever paid as GLP-1 speakers were mostly first paid before 2015, so they are outside the event study. The results describe doctors first reached by a lunch, not speakers.

## Result 1: the paid brand gains share

Among doctors who already prescribe GLP-1s (@fig-hero, top of page), the paid brand's share of their GLP-1 claims rises after the first payment and keeps rising for two to three years. Averaged over the four years from the payment year on, the gain is **{{< var share_trulicity >}} percentage points for Trulicity, {{< var share_ozempic >}} for Ozempic and {{< var share_mounjaro >}} for Mounjaro** (measured from its 2022 launch).

For Trulicity and Mounjaro, the paid and comparison doctors' shares moved together beforehand (pre-trend test p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity >}} and {{< var share_pre_mounjaro >}}). For Ozempic there was a mild upward drift before payment (p = {{< var share_pre_ozempic >}}) that disappears with matching.

**The gain comes from direct competitors.** After a Trulicity payment, Victoza's share falls by {{< var src_tru_vic >}} points; after an Ozempic payment, Trulicity's falls by {{< var src_oz_tru >}}; after a Mounjaro payment, Lilly's own Trulicity falls by {{< var src_mj_tru >}}. For the established brands, {{< var switch_frac_trulicity >}}% (Trulicity) and {{< var switch_frac_ozempic >}}% (Ozempic) of the extra claims after payment come from switching between brands rather than from more GLP-1 prescribing overall.

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart5_share_dumbbells.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart5_share_dumbbells_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
:::

**Victoza is the exception.** Its share *falls* after a Victoza payment ({{< var share_victoza >}} points). Those payments came while Novo Nordisk was moving the market from Victoza to its own newer Ozempic.

::: {.doesnt-box}
**How strong is this?** Under the linear estimators the share gain is precise and survives matching and adjustment for each doctor's starting brand mix. The pre-registered version models the share on a log-odds scale with matching. It gives similar sizes ({{< var frac_trulicity >}}, {{< var frac_ozempic >}}, {{< var frac_mounjaro >}}), but it is much less precise, and only Mounjaro's interval excludes zero on its own. Pooled across brands it is {{< var h5 >}} points (Holm-adjusted p = {{< var h5_holm >}}). Without matching, the log-odds version is close to zero. So the direction is consistent; the size depends on modelling choices, and the pooled test rests on matching.
:::

## Result 2: the volume increase mostly reflects who gets paid

The obvious headline would be that paid doctors become far more likely to prescribe the brand. They do: the probability of writing at least 11 claims of the paid brand in a year rises by **{{< var att_trulicity >}} points for Trulicity, {{< var att_victoza >}} for Victoza and {{< var att_ozempic >}} for Ozempic** over the four years from the first payment, and matching on prior prescribing barely changes that ({{< var matched_trulicity >}} / {{< var matched_victoza >}} / {{< var matched_ozempic >}}).

But the pre-registered tests say this number cannot be read as the effect of a payment:

::: {#fig-statins .column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart1b_targeting_statins.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}

![](figures/final/chart1b_targeting_statins_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}

The paid brand and statins around the first payment. Data: [falsification.json](qa/falsification.json).
:::

- **Paid doctors were already rising before they were paid.** The pre-payment trend is steep and statistically clear for all three brands.
- **Their statin prescribing rises too**: by {{< var statin_trulicity >}}, {{< var statin_victoza >}} and {{< var statin_ozempic >}} points, with an even steeper rise beforehand. A GLP-1 lunch has no reason to change statin prescribing; a growing practice does. Paid doctors' total Medicare Part D claims grew {{< var total_claims_growth >}}% more than their comparison doctors'.
- **Matching does not remove it.** Matching on prior brand prescribing balances those variables (largest standardised difference {{< var own_smd >}}), but not total practice growth (standardised difference {{< var growth_smd >}}). Matching on practice growth as well leaves the estimates almost unchanged ({{< var dev8_trulicity >}} / {{< var dev8_victoza >}} / {{< var dev8_ozempic >}}), and the statin test still fails under it.

Under the pre-registered interpretation rules, this pattern is reported as **"explained at least partly by targeting of already-rising prescribers."** It is why the article leads with brand share, which a growing practice does not move.

## Result 3: bigger payments, bigger changes, different doctors

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart2_dose.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart2_dose_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
:::

Doctors who received $100 or more for the brand in their first payment year rose more than those who received less: {{< var dose_ge100_trulicity >}} vs {{< var dose_lt100_trulicity >}} points for Trulicity, {{< var dose_ge100_ozempic >}} vs {{< var dose_lt100_ozempic >}} for Ozempic. Doctors with four or more contacts in that year rose about twice as much as doctors with one ({{< var contacts4_trulicity >}} vs {{< var contacts1_trulicity >}}; {{< var contacts4_ozempic >}} vs {{< var contacts1_ozempic >}}). Pooled, the $100 gap is {{< var h4 >}} points.

**This is a gradient, not a dose-response.** Companies give more to doctors they expect more from, so the higher-paid groups differ in ways the comparison cannot fully remove.

**Speaker fees vs meals.** Doctors first paid with a speaker or consulting fee rose {{< var h2 >}} points more than meal-only doctors, but there are only {{< var n_fee_first >}} such doctors per brand, and the difference is not statistically clear after adjustment for multiple tests (Holm p = {{< var h2_holm >}}). The study cannot say whether speaker fees matter more than meals.

## Where the money goes

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart7_lorenz.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart7_lorenz >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart7_lorenz_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart7_lorenz >}}"}
:::

GLP-1 promotional money is extremely concentrated. Of {{< var n_paid_lorenz >}} prescribers paid for a GLP-1 through 2024, the top 1% received {{< var top1_share >}}% of the dollars and the top 10% received {{< var top10_share >}}% (Gini {{< var gini >}}); the median paid prescriber received ${{< var median_usd >}} over twelve years. Speaker and consulting fees are {{< var fees_share >}}% of all GLP-1 promotional dollars, paid to {{< var glp1_speakers >}} speakers in all; meals are {{< var meal_share >}}%.

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart6_state_map.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart6_state_map >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart6_state_map_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart6_state_map >}}"}
:::

Per Medicare Part D enrollee with diabetes, GLP-1 promotional payments in 2024 ranged from ${{< var state_min >}} ({{< var state_min_name >}}) to ${{< var state_max >}} ({{< var state_max_name >}}), against ${{< var state_us >}} nationally. {{< var masked_states >}} are left blank: in each, one prescriber received more than half of the state's GLP-1 promotional dollars, so the state's figure would describe one person.

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart8_specialty.png){.light-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart8_specialty >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart8_specialty_dark.png){.dark-content fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart8_specialty >}}"}
:::

Relative to diabetes workload, endocrinologists receive about {{< var endo_ratio >}} times as much per claim as primary-care physicians (${{< var endo_per_1000 >}} vs ${{< var pc_per_1000 >}} per 1,000 other diabetes-drug claims in 2024).

## Who responds

The pre-registered secondary questions, each adjusted together for multiple testing [@holm1979]:

::: {.table-scroll}
| Question | Estimate | Holm-adjusted p | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speaker or consulting fee vs meals only | {{< var h2 >}} pp | {{< var h2_holm >}} | Not supported: too few fee recipients |
| Specialists vs primary care | {{< var h3 >}} pp | {{< var h3_holm >}} | Not supported |
| First-year $100 or more vs under $100 | {{< var h4 >}} pp | {{< var h4_holm_fmt >}} | Gradient; higher-paid doctors are more selected |
| Paid brand's share (log-odds, matched) | {{< var h5 >}} pp | {{< var h5_holm >}} | Supported, pooled; rests on matching |
| 30-day fills (most conservative suppression bound) | {{< var h6 >}}% | {{< var h6_holm_fmt >}} | Supported; size depends on how hidden cells are bounded ({{< var h6_min >}}% to {{< var h6_max >}}%) |
| Nurse practitioners and physician assistants | {{< var h7 >}} pp | {{< var h7_holm_fmt >}} | Supported, with the same targeting caveat |

: Secondary hypotheses. Data: [secondary_family.csv](qa/secondary_family.csv). {tbl-colwidths="[34,14,14,38]"}
:::

**Region and setting.** The increase is larger in the South than in every other region, for every brand (by {{< var south_gap >}} points), and larger in rural than urban practices for Trulicity ({{< var rural_trulicity >}}) and Victoza ({{< var rural_victoza >}}). These subgroup estimates inherit the targeting caveat above: they may reflect where practices were growing, or regional formularies, rather than who responds to payments.

**Specialty.** There is no consistent specialist advantage. Victoza's increase is larger among endocrinologists ({{< var victoza_endo >}} points relative to primary care), while Ozempic's is smaller among endocrinologists ({{< var oz_endo >}}) and cardiologists ({{< var oz_cardio >}}).

**Nurse practitioners and physician assistants**, whose payments are reported only from 2021, show increases of {{< var h7_trulicity >}} (Trulicity) and {{< var h7_ozempic >}} (Ozempic) points; Victoza has only {{< var h7_victoza_n >}} newly paid NPs and PAs. There is no matched or negative-control version of this estimate.

## Falsification and robustness

::: {.table-scroll}
| Test | What would sink the finding | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-payment trend, ≥ 11 claims | Paid doctors already rising | **Fails**: steep rising trend for all three brands |
| Pre-payment trend, brand share | Share already rising | **Passes** for Trulicity (p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity >}}) and Mounjaro (p = {{< var share_pre_mounjaro >}}); mild drift for Ozempic |
| Statins (negative-control outcome) | Statins rise too | **Fails** for all three: {{< var statin_trulicity >}} / {{< var statin_victoza >}} / {{< var statin_ozempic >}} pp |
| Anticoagulant payments (negative-control exposure) | Unrelated payments predict GLP-1 growth as strongly | **Passes**, but still {{< var nc_anticoag_ratio >}}% of the GLP-1 association |
| Inhaled-respiratory payments (second negative-control exposure) | Same | **Fails** ({{< var nc_inhaled_ratio >}}%); AstraZeneca and GSK also sell GLP-1s |
| Fake payment dates one or two years early | "Effects" before the real payment | **Passes** (at most {{< var placebo_max >}} pp) |
| Ozempic payment → Trulicity prescribing (placebo brand) | Competitor rises too | **Fails** in levels ({{< var placebo_brand_oz >}} pp), but Trulicity's *share* falls |
| HonestDiD sensitivity | Small violations of parallel trends erase it | Survives violations up to {{< var honest_trulicity >}}× / {{< var honest_victoza >}}× / {{< var honest_ozempic >}}× the largest pre-period deviation |
| {{< var n_specs >}} alternative specifications | Effect depends on choices | Stays positive and above the 2-point threshold of interest in all: {{< var sens_trulicity >}} / {{< var sens_victoza >}} / {{< var sens_ozempic >}} pp |

: Falsification and robustness for Trulicity / Victoza / Ozempic. Data: [falsification.csv](qa/falsification.csv), [sensitivity.csv](qa/sensitivity.csv). {tbl-colwidths="[30,30,40]"}
:::

The failures all point the same way: paid doctors run larger and faster-growing practices. They undermine the volume result, which is why it is reported as targeting, and they leave the brand-share result standing, because a growing practice raises every brand together.

## Limitations

- **Targeting is not ruled out, only partly removed.** Matching balances prior brand prescribing but not overall practice growth, and the statin test fails even when matched on growth. Brand share removes practice size, but representatives may also visit when a brand wins a formulary or guideline change, which would raise its share without the payment doing anything.
- **The share result is modest and model-dependent.** It is precise under the linear estimators but imprecise under the pre-registered log-odds form, where only Mounjaro is clear on its own.
- **Annual data blur timing.** Payments arrive during the year, so the payment year is partly before and partly after.
- **Suppression.** Medicare hides prescriber-drug rows under 11 claims. The binary outcome is fully observed, but prescription volumes depend on how hidden cells are bounded.
- **Who is studied.** Medicare Part D only (not commercial insurance or Medicaid); physicians first reached mostly by sponsored meals; nurse practitioners and physician assistants only from 2021.
- **Spillovers.** Payments to one doctor may change colleagues' prescribing [@agha2022; @hyman2025]. Comparison doctors in practices where nobody was paid give *larger* estimates, so spillovers would bias the main estimate down, not up.

## Ethics: why no individual doctors appear

Open Payments names every recipient, and it would be easy to publish a league table. This project deliberately does not. A payment is legal, and a doctor who prescribes a paid brand may be prescribing well; a ranking would invite conclusions about individuals that aggregate data cannot support. Every published figure and table aggregates at least 11 prescribers per cell. Geographic cells are also withheld when one prescriber received more than half of the dollars, so that no state or specialty figure describes one person. Code uses prescriber identifiers internally; nothing released contains them.

## Reproducibility

All data are public. The pipeline (Python 3.12, DuckDB; R only for cross-checking the estimators) rebuilds every number and figure from the raw federal files with one command, `make all`, in about two hours. Two independent rebuilds produce identical results. Every number in this article is read from the pipeline's QA outputs, never typed by hand, and a test fails if one is. Code, pre-registration, deviations and the QA report: [github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1](https://github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1).

**What is new here.** Earlier work, including the closest design [@carey2021], established that payments and prescribing go together, but mostly from cross-sectional snapshots of older drugs. This project follows every Medicare GLP-1 prescriber brand by brand over twelve years, uses estimators built for staggered timing, tests brand switching directly, and reports the negative controls that cut against its own headline.
